templates.pattern: A wave has a time period of [T] ms. Calculate the frequency of the wave in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Period in seconds = [T] ms ÷ 1000 = [T/1000] s
Frequency = 1 ÷ period
= 1 ÷ ([T] ÷ 1000)
= 1000 ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] Hz

Always convert milliseconds to seconds before applying f = 1/T.

templates.pattern: A sound source emitting [F] Hz moves toward a stationary observer at [VS] m/s. The speed of sound is [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency heard by the observer in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Doppler effect — source approaching:
f' = f × v ÷ (v − vs)
= [F] × [V] ÷ ([V] − [VS])
= [F] × [V] ÷ [V-VS]
= [RESULT] Hz

The observed frequency is higher than the emitted frequency when the source approaches. This is why a siren sounds higher pitched as it approaches.

templates.pattern: A sound source emitting [F] Hz moves away from a stationary observer at [VS] m/s. The speed of sound is [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency heard by the observer in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Doppler effect — source receding:
f' = f × v ÷ (v + vs)
= [F] × [V] ÷ ([V] + [VS])
= [F] × [V] ÷ [V+VS]
= [RESULT] Hz

The observed frequency is lower than the emitted frequency when the source moves away. This is why a siren sounds lower pitched as it moves away.

templates.pattern: Sound intensity at a distance of [D1] m from a source is [I] W/m². Calculate the intensity at a distance of [D2] m from the same source in W/m².
templates.explanation:
Inverse square law:
I₁d₁² = I₂d₂²
I₂ = I₁ × d₁² ÷ d₂²
= [I] × [D1]² ÷ [D2]²
= [I] × [D1*D1] ÷ [D2*D2]
= [RESULT] W/m²

Sound intensity decreases with the square of distance. Doubling the distance reduces intensity to one quarter.

templates.pattern: A wave passes from medium 1 where its speed is [V1] m/s into medium 2 where its speed is [V2] m/s. The original wavelength is [L1] m. Calculate the new wavelength in medium 2 in metres.
templates.explanation:
Frequency stays constant at a boundary.
λ₂ = λ₁ × v₂ ÷ v₁
= [L1] × [V2] ÷ [V1]
= [RESULT] m

When a wave enters a new medium its speed and wavelength change but its frequency remains the same.

templates.pattern: A standing wave is set up on a string of length [L] m fixed at both ends. Calculate the wavelength of the fundamental frequency in metres.
templates.explanation:
For the fundamental (first harmonic) on a string fixed at both ends:
λ = 2L
= 2 × [L]
= [RESULT] m

At the fundamental frequency exactly half a wavelength fits along the string length. The two fixed ends are always nodes.

templates.pattern: A string of length [L] m is fixed at both ends and has a wave speed of [V] m/s. Calculate the fundamental frequency of the string in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Fundamental frequency f = v ÷ 2L
= [V] ÷ (2 × [L])
= [V] ÷ [2*L]
= [RESULT] Hz

This is the lowest frequency at which the string can resonate. Higher harmonics occur at integer multiples of this frequency.

templates.pattern: A pipe open at both ends has a length of [L] m. The speed of sound is [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency of the second harmonic of the pipe in Hz.
templates.explanation:
For an open pipe the second harmonic frequency f₂ = v ÷ L
= [V] ÷ [L]
= [RESULT] Hz

For an open pipe: f₁ = v/2L, f₂ = v/L, f₃ = 3v/2L. Both ends are always antinodes. All harmonics are present.

templates.pattern: A pipe closed at one end has a length of [L] m. The speed of sound is [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency of the third harmonic of the pipe in Hz.
templates.explanation:
For a closed pipe the third harmonic frequency f₃ = 3v ÷ 4L
= 3 × [V] ÷ (4 × [L])
= [3*V] ÷ [4*L]
= [RESULT] Hz

For a closed pipe only odd harmonics are present: f₁ = v/4L, f₃ = 3v/4L, f₅ = 5v/4L. The closed end is always a node.

templates.pattern: A wave enters a new medium and its speed increases from [V1] m/s to [V2] m/s. The frequency remains constant at [F] Hz. Calculate the wavelength in the new medium in metres.
templates.explanation:
Wavelength in new medium = new speed ÷ frequency
= v₂ ÷ f
= [V2] ÷ [F]
= [RESULT] m

Frequency never changes when a wave crosses a boundary. Only speed and wavelength change.
